content: Aluminium phosphate (AlPO4) is a chemical compound that exists in various forms, both natural and synthetic. The anhydrous form of aluminium phosphate occurs naturally as the mineral berlinite. Synthetic anhydrous forms of aluminium phosphate are also widely known, and they possess framework structures similar to zeolites. These synthetic forms are often utilized as catalysts or molecular sieves. The dihydrate form of aluminium phosphate, AlPO4·2H2O, is found in nature as the minerals variscite and meta-variscite. Additionally, a synthetic hydrated form, AlPO4·1.5H2O, has been developed. Commercially, aluminium phosphate is available in gel form. Aluminium phosphate, specifically berlinite, is isoelectronic with silicon dioxide (SiO2). Berlinite visually resembles quartz and has a structural similarity to quartz, with silicon atoms replaced by aluminium and phosphorus atoms. The structure consists of alternating AlO4 and PO4 tetrahedra. Like quartz, berlinite exhibits chirality and piezoelectric properties. When crystalline berlinite is subjected to heat, it transitions into the tridymite and cristobalite forms, a behavior that parallels that of silicon dioxide. The dihydrate form of aluminium phosphate, represented by the minerals variscite and meta-variscite, has a structure composed of phosphate anions, aluminium cations, and water molecules. In this structure, the aluminium cations are coordinated to six surrounding atoms. Aluminophosphate molecular sieves, commonly referred to as ALPOs, are a class of materials with microporous framework structures. These materials were first reported in 1982 and share the same chemical composition of AlPO4. Their frameworks are constructed from alternating AlO4 and PO4 tetrahedra, similar to berlinite. However, unlike berlinite, these frameworks contain microporous cavities of varying sizes, depending on the orientation of the tetrahedra. This variability in cavity size is analogous to aluminosilicate zeolites, although aluminophosphates lack the electrically charged frameworks characteristic of zeolites. The synthesis of aluminophosphate molecular sieves typically involves the hydrothermal reaction of phosphoric acid with an aluminium source, such as aluminium hydroxide, aluminium nitrate, or aluminium alkoxide, under controlled pH conditions. Organic amines, known as structure-directing agents (SDAs), are used during the synthesis to guide the formation of the porous framework. In the medical field, aluminium phosphate gel is employed as an adsorbent for toxoids. In its dried form, which contains hydrated AlPO4, it is used as an antacid. Industrially, the Al-PO4-H2O system serves as the foundation for various adhesives, binders, and cements. In geologically stable regions, such as Australia and Southern Africa, aluminium phosphate is often the predominant form of phosphorus in soils. This occurs because phosphate in rainwater reacts with dissolved aluminium in the soil to form aluminium phosphate. Although it is not as insoluble as other soil components in these regions, aluminium phosphate can form highly insoluble double salts, known as taranakites, with essential plant nutrients like potassium and nitrogen. In coastal areas of South Africa and Namibia, the combination of ancient soils and high phosphate input from nutrient-rich oceans driven by the Benguela Current leads to the accumulation of aluminium phosphate, forming concentrated deposits known as aluminium phosphate rock. While these deposits have only recently garnered interest for agricultural phosphorus extraction, they hold significant economic potential if cost-effective processing methods are developed.
